market_summary:
U.S. equities staged a sharp rebound after a risk-off midweek drawdown tied to escalating U.S.–Iran tensions and hotter inflation prints. Index futures and cash markets bounced as the U.S. signaled an end to the latest round of strikes on Iran, oil prices eased back from recent highs, and investors refocused on resilient growth and AI-led earnings strength.[8][9][23] Tech and software led the rally, with AI infrastructure, cybersecurity, and enterprise software materially outperforming as names like SNOW, OKTA, MU, APP, TEAM, NOW, and ORCL posted outsized gains, while laggards clustered in defensives, energy, and selected materials.

Factor-wise, the tape showed a renewed preference for high-growth, high-beta software and semis, amid strong AI demand signals from Micron, CrowdStrike, Palo Alto Networks, and ServiceNow, even as idiosyncratic blowups like ZS and Oracle reminded investors that expectations are elevated.[28][32][33][40] Into the coming fortnight, the focus shifts back to the macro path for inflation, the Fed reaction function, and whether AI-driven earnings upgrades can offset geopolitics and higher-for-longer rate fears, with volatility modestly elevated as VIX hovers in the low 20s.[5][9]

value_picks.name: The Walt Disney Company
value_picks.why_undervalued: Disney is trading at a modest earnings multiple relative to its history and to high-quality media peers, despite having restructured its cost base and refocused on core franchises.[13] The market remains skeptical about the profitability of its streaming operations and the long-term trajectory of traditional linear TV, which keeps a lid on the valuation multiple.[13] Sentiment has also been weighed down by concerns over cyclical parks attendance and content spending volatility, even as the company has demonstrated operating discipline. This combination of franchise strength and depressed sentiment creates a valuation gap that appears wider than the underlying fundamentals justify.
value_picks.bull_case: The bull case hinges on Disney successfully scaling its streaming platforms to sustainable profitability while using its unrivaled content library to drive pricing power and engagement.[13] As cost synergies from restructuring flow through, margin recovery in both the media and parks businesses could surprise to the upside, reinforcing confidence in cash flow durability. A clearer capital allocation framework, including measured buybacks and a steadily growing dividend, would further support a re-rating toward a premium media and consumer brands multiple. Over time, investor perception could shift from viewing Disney as a challenged legacy media company to a diversified, IP-rich platform with multiple monetization levers across experiences, consumer products, and digital distribution.
value_picks.key_risks: A key risk is that streaming economics remain structurally weaker than anticipated, with elevated content costs and intense competition preventing Disney from achieving attractive long-term margins. If cord-cutting accelerates faster than Disney can offset with direct-to-consumer revenue, overall media segment cash flows could compress, undermining the investment case. Parks and experiences are also economically sensitive, so a global slowdown or geopolitical disruptions could pressure high-margin resort and cruise revenue. Finally, regulatory or political controversies around content and branding could weigh on audience reach and brand equity, which would be particularly damaging for a company whose valuation rests heavily on its intellectual property.

value_picks.name: Comcast Corporation
value_picks.why_undervalued: Comcast trades at a very low earnings multiple around the mid-single digits, significantly below the broader market despite its stable cash-generating cable and broadband franchises.[25] The stock is hovering only modestly above its 52-week low and roughly 30% below its 52-week high, indicating pronounced investor pessimism.[25] The market is focused on secular cord-cutting pressures in video and regulatory overhangs, while arguably underappreciating the resilience and pricing power of its connectivity and business services segments. This has left Comcast valued more like a melting-ice-cube legacy telecom than a diversified communications and media infrastructure business with strong free cash generation.[25]
value_picks.bull_case: The bull case centers on Comcast’s ability to continue growing high-margin broadband and business services while managing the decline in legacy video subscribers. If management prioritizes shareholder returns through a combination of its sizable dividend and opportunistic buybacks funded by robust free cash flow, the yield plus capital return could become a key driver of total return. Over time, incremental monetization of its network through speed tiers, bundled offerings, and enterprise solutions could stabilize or grow EBITDA even in a mature market. As investors gain confidence that broadband cash flows are durable and not as threatened by competition as feared, the equity could re-rate closer to a high-single-digit or low double-digit multiple, delivering meaningful upside from depressed levels.[25][30]
value_picks.key_risks: The primary risk is that competitive intensity in broadband increases more than expected, whether from fiber overbuilds, fixed wireless access, or new technologies, which could erode Comcast’s pricing power. If regulators constrain pricing or impose additional network obligations, the returns on incremental capital investment might compress, reducing the appeal of the infrastructure asset base. Weakness in NBCUniversal and media properties, including advertising cyclicality and audience fragmentation, could also pressure consolidated results and muddy the narrative around Comcast as a defensive cash generator. Additionally, any missteps in capital allocation, such as expensive content or M&A bets, could crowd out shareholder returns and reinforce the market’s skepticism toward management.

value_picks.name: AT&T Inc.
value_picks.why_undervalued: AT&T trades at a mid-single-digit earnings multiple, reflecting deep investor skepticism about its leverage, capital intensity, and long-term growth prospects.[26] Despite posting strong free cash flow in recent quarters and demonstrating progress on deleveraging, the valuation continues to embed a heavy discount relative to both its history and peers.[26][31] The market is preoccupied with the risk that elevated network investment and spectrum spending will permanently suppress returns, even as management prioritizes cash generation and debt paydown. This disconnect between improving fundamentals and persistently low expectations positions AT&T as a classic value name where sentiment has arguably overshot to the downside.[26][31]
value_picks.bull_case: The bull case rests on AT&T continuing to execute on its simplified strategy as a focused connectivity provider, steadily expanding 5G and fiber while converting that investment into stable ARPU and subscriber growth. If free cash flow remains robust and management consistently allocates excess cash to debt reduction and a sustainable dividend, equity holders could benefit from both yield and gradual multiple expansion. Stronger-than-expected uptake in fiber, coupled with disciplined pricing in wireless, could reinforce the perception that AT&T’s asset base is more durable and less commoditized than bears assume. Over time, a cleaner balance sheet and clearer capital return policy could shift the narrative from distressed telecom to a stable infrastructure-like cash flow stream warranting a higher valuation.[26][31]
value_picks.key_risks: Key risks include the possibility that competitive dynamics in wireless and broadband force AT&T into price wars, undermining margins and slowing deleveraging progress. If required capital expenditure and spectrum costs remain structurally high, free cash flow could fall short of expectations, calling into question the sustainability of both the dividend and the value thesis. Regulatory or legal challenges, including those related to legacy liabilities or network build-out obligations, could introduce additional cash demands or strategic constraints. Moreover, any execution missteps in retiring debt, simplifying the portfolio, or integrating network deployments could erode investor confidence and prolong the stock’s low-multiple status.[26][31]

value_picks.name: Synchrony Financial
value_picks.why_undervalued: Synchrony Financial trades at a low single-digit earnings multiple relative to the broader market, reflecting concerns about consumer credit quality and the cyclicality of its private-label and co-brand card portfolios.[34] The market appears to be pricing in a potential deterioration in credit performance as macro conditions evolve, despite the company’s track record of managing risk through underwriting and reserve builds.[34] As a result, Synchrony’s valuation implies a stressed scenario that may not fully reflect the diversity of its partnerships across retail, health, and other verticals. This gap between the price and the company’s normalized earnings power presents an opportunity for value-oriented investors willing to underwrite through the cycle.[34]
value_picks.bull_case: The bull case for Synchrony assumes that credit normalization progresses in a manageable fashion, with loss rates rising but remaining within historically acceptable bounds. If the company can continue to grow receivables and fee income through new partnerships and deeper penetration of existing relationships, earnings could prove more resilient than the current multiple suggests.[34] Strong capital generation and prudent balance sheet management would allow Synchrony to return excess capital via buybacks and dividends, enhancing per-share growth even in a moderate macro environment. Over time, markets could reward the company for its diversified funding base and risk management capabilities, leading to a re-rating more in line with other profitable consumer finance names.[34]
value_picks.key_risks: The principal risk is a sharper-than-expected downturn in consumer credit quality, particularly in lower-FICO or more discretionary spending categories, which could drive higher charge-offs and provisioning needs. If unemployment rises or consumer balance sheets weaken meaningfully, Synchrony’s earnings could be hit hard, undermining confidence in its through-the-cycle profitability. Regulatory changes that tighten consumer lending standards or cap fees and charges could also impair the economics of its card and financing products. In addition, concentration with a handful of large retail partners exposes Synchrony to renegotiation risk or the potential loss of key agreements, which could pressure growth and margins.[34]

value_picks.name: Netflix, Inc.
value_picks.why_undervalued: Netflix shares are trading roughly 36% below their 52-week high and only modestly above their 52-week low, despite the company generating substantial free cash flow and expanding operating margins.[27][19] The market appears concerned that subscriber growth is maturing and that competitive pressures from other streaming platforms will limit pricing power and content returns. Yet Netflix continues to add subscribers globally and is leveraging its scale in content and technology to drive efficiency, which is not fully reflected in the current share price. This disconnect suggests investors may be overemphasizing the risk of saturation while underweighting the company’s demonstrated ability to monetize its large, engaged user base.[27][19]
value_picks.bull_case: The bull case is that Netflix continues to execute on its strategy of balancing growth with profitability, using its scale to amortize content costs over a vast subscriber base. Initiatives such as password-sharing crackdowns, ad-supported tiers, and localized content can provide incremental revenue and margin expansion, supporting a structurally higher free cash flow profile.[19][27] As investors gain confidence that Netflix can sustain operating margins above 30% while still growing subscribers and ARPU, the stock could re-rate to reflect a more mature, high-quality media and technology franchise. Additionally, optionality in areas like gaming, merchandising, and live content could add new revenue streams that the market currently assigns little value.[19][27]
value_picks.key_risks: The main risk is that content spending must remain elevated to defend market share, leading to a resurgence in cash burn and disappointing free cash flow relative to current expectations. If competition intensifies, with rivals willing to subsidize streaming through broader ecosystems, Netflix’s pricing power and subscriber growth could come under pressure. Regulatory challenges in key markets, including potential rules on local content or data usage, could increase costs or constrain flexibility. Moreover, if consumers become more price sensitive and rotate among services, churn could rise and undermine the perceived durability of Netflix’s subscription base.[27][19]

momentum_picks.name: Hilton Grand Vacations Inc.
momentum_picks.catalyst: Hilton Grand Vacations is benefiting from solid leisure travel demand and the ongoing normalization of timeshare usage and vacation patterns after several years of disruption, which is supporting both higher occupancy and improved pricing power.[1][20] Zacks highlights HGV on its June 2026 "Best Stocks to Buy Now" list, citing a roughly 145% projected EPS growth and more than 11% projected sales growth over the next year, which underpins the stock’s strong 12-week price momentum of about 20.8%.[1][20]
momentum_picks.risk_reward: At the current price, investors are paying a single-digit forward P/E for a company with strong expected earnings and double-digit projected revenue growth, offering an attractive risk/reward if management delivers on growth and margin expansion targets outlined by analysts.[1][20] If travel demand remains resilient and HGV continues to execute on its pipeline of resort openings and member acquisition, there is room for multiple expansion alongside earnings growth, which could sustain the stock’s positive momentum.[1][6][20]
momentum_picks.key_risks: The primary risks include a macroeconomic slowdown that could pressure discretionary vacation spending, leading to softer bookings and timeshare sales, which would directly challenge the bullish growth assumptions baked into current estimates.[1][20] Additionally, higher interest rates or tighter credit conditions could hurt financing for timeshare purchases and elevate default risk in the loan portfolio, while any operational issues or negative headlines around timeshare practices could weigh on brand perception and sales conversion rates.[1][20]

momentum_picks.catalyst: Marathon Petroleum is riding strong refining margins and disciplined capital allocation, including buybacks and dividends, which are supporting earnings growth and share price momentum.[1][7][20] The stock appears on Zacks’ June 2026 best stocks list with a roughly 11.5% 12-week price gain, an attractive forward P/E under 9, and projected EPS growth near 181% with approximately 5.8% projected sales growth over the next year, pointing to a powerful fundamental backdrop for the current move.[1][7][20][28]
momentum_picks.risk_reward: From the current price level and valuation, the risk/reward remains favorable if refining crack spreads stay healthy and management continues deploying excess cash to repurchases and debt reduction, sustaining high returns on capital.[1][7][20][28] However, given the cyclical nature of refining and the stock’s strong recent run, investors should expect elevated volatility, but long-term energy demand and tight capacity can still justify further upside if the cycle remains supportive.[3][11][25]
momentum_picks.key_risks: Key risks include a sharp compression in refining margins if product demand weakens or if new capacity comes online, which would pressure earnings and could quickly reverse the stock’s momentum.[3][7][11][25] Regulatory and environmental policy changes, potential accidents or unplanned outages at refineries, and commodity price swings, particularly in crude oil differentials, could all materially affect profitability and investor sentiment toward the stock.[3][7][25][28]

momentum_picks.catalyst: Diversified Energy appears on the Zacks best stocks list despite recent price softness, reflecting investor interest in its yield, asset base, and potential for operational efficiencies even amid currently negative projected sales growth.[1][20] The company’s strategy of acquiring mature producing assets and optimizing decline profiles can create stable cash flows, and if management can arrest the projected revenue contraction of roughly 17% while maintaining distributions, the stock could see renewed momentum from current levels.[1][20]

narrative:
# US Equity Weekly: AI Momentum, Factor Whiplash, And The Return Of Rate Sensitivity

The past week in US equities was defined by an intense tug-of-war between surging artificial intelligence–linked growth names, a powerful catch-up move in legacy software and cyclicals, and a renewed reminder from the macro tape that rates and labor data still matter. An early-week risk-on tone helped propel the S&P 500 to yet another record close and extend its advance to a nine-session winning streak, supported by broad strength in semiconductors and select enterprise software and cybersecurity leaders.[1][20] As the week progressed, however, a stronger-than-expected jobs backdrop and rising rate expectations reignited pressure on long-duration tech, triggering a sharp factor reversal that hit the Nasdaq 100 and the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index particularly hard, even as underlying AI adoption and earnings delivery remained robust.[4][20] Within this macro and factor cross-current, our watchlist saw outsized moves in both directions: Snowflake, Okta, Micron, AppLovin, Atlassian, ServiceNow, Oracle, IBM and a broad cohort of data, security, and infrastructure names delivered 10–50 percent weekly gains, while Zscaler and a subset of semis and defensives suffered double-digit drawdowns amid profit-taking and rotation. Against a backdrop of stable but elevated inflation expectations and a policy path that still points to restrictive rates through year-end, the equity market remains anchored by AI-driven earnings revisions, but with materially higher intra-week volatility and greater dispersion at the single-stock level.[2][3][25]

## Market Overview

US large-cap equities entered the week with strong upward momentum, culminating in the S&P 500 on track for, and ultimately achieving, its ninth straight day of gains and another record close.[1] On the day highlighted in Bloomberg’s closing coverage, the S&P 500 added roughly 0.1 percent, enough to set a fresh record high, while the Nasdaq Composite registered a more meaningful gain and the Russell 2000 small-cap index outperformed on a relative basis with a rise of about 0.9 percent.[1] This pattern reflected both the continued strength of mega-cap technology and the beginnings of a catch-up trade in more cyclically sensitive and domestically oriented names, particularly in industrials, energy, materials, and select financials.[1] Sector breadth improved markedly, with traditionally defensive utilities gaining close to 1.9 percent on the day, materials up more than 1 percent, and energy similarly higher, even as communication services lagged and finished down about 2.6 percent as investors rotated away from some of the year’s most crowded trades.[1]

This constructive breadth and record-setting headline performance were underpinned by a powerful move in semiconductors, where the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index extended gains into the close and finished that session higher by approximately 5.4 percent.[1] That move came on top of extraordinary twelve-month performance, with the PHLX Semiconductor Index up about 132.8 percent over the past year and trading near 12,206, reflecting the structurally bullish consensus around AI compute demand and memory pricing.[20] High-profile individual winners included Hewlett Packard Enterprise, which surged roughly 19 percent on the day and had been up as much as 37 percent intraday after issuing an AI-infrastructure-driven revenue outlook that exceeded analyst expectations, reinforcing the market’s appetite for earnings-backed AI narratives.[1] The broader tape during this phase displayed what we would characterize as an “AI plus cyclicals” pattern: AI beneficiaries continued to lead, but they were increasingly joined by traditional sectors that benefit from improving growth and capex cycles.

The tone shifted meaningfully later in the week following a stronger labor-market print and associated repricing of policy expectations. Bloomberg’s mid-week coverage framed the session as a tech-led selloff triggered by a robust jobs report that lifted yields and reignited talk of additional Federal Reserve tightening.[4] On that day, the Nasdaq 100 fell roughly 3.9 percent, the Nasdaq Composite lost about 3.5 percent, and the S&P 500 dropped around 2 percent, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average declined by close to 0.9 percent.[4] The damage was most acute in high-beta technology and semiconductors: Micron, Nvidia, Broadcom, and Advanced Micro Devices each saw intraday declines between roughly 5 and 9 percent, and the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index dropped by approximately 8.5 percent as investors unwound some of the most extended AI and chip trades.[4] This rapid reversal underscored the fragility of sentiment when valuations, positioning, and rate expectations are all stretched at the same time.

The rate backdrop provides important context for these swings. Treasury yields moved sharply higher alongside the jobs data, with the 10-year yield quoted around 4.54 percent, the 2-year near 4.16 percent, and the 30-year close to 5.00 percent in Bloomberg’s coverage of the selloff session.[4] In parallel, forward-looking expectations tracked by Trading Economics show that the federal funds rate is still projected to end the current quarter around 3.75 percent, implying a path of gradual easing from today’s restrictive levels but not an imminent pivot to aggressive cuts.[2] That combination—elevated but potentially past-peak policy rates, rising long-end yields, and re-acceleration signals from labor and growth—continues to place long-duration, high-multiple growth equities at the center of macro volatility. Against this backdrop, investors are increasingly differentiating between AI-related names with visible, near-term earnings leverage and those whose narratives remain more speculative.

From a style perspective, this week delivered classic factor whiplash. Early in the period, growth, momentum, and quality factors outperformed, supported by mega-cap technology, secular software leaders, and AI infrastructure plays. As yields jumped, there was an abrupt rotation toward value, cyclicals, financials, and shorter-duration cash-flow stories, which helped limit the downside in the S&P 500 even as the Nasdaq bore the brunt of the selloff.[4] Small caps, represented by the Russell 2000’s intraday gain of about 0.9 percent on one of the up days, began to show tentative leadership, although the sustainability of that trend will depend heavily on how financing conditions evolve and whether the recent uptick in inflation proves transitory or persistent.[1][25] Overall, the week ended with equities still near highs, but with higher realized volatility and wider dispersion across sectors and single names, setting the stage for a more tactical trading environment through the remainder of the quarter.

## Sector Leadership & Rotation

The most striking feature of sector performance this week was the continued centrality of AI and digital transformation themes, but expressed through a broader set of vehicles beyond the core megacap complex. Semiconductors remained a key driver: the PHLX Semiconductor Index’s roughly 5.4 percent gain on one of the record-setting sessions, and its approximately 132.8 percent one-year performance, reflected sustained optimism around data-center AI, high-bandwidth memory, and advanced packaging demand.[1][20] At the same time, the violent pullback later in the week, with the same semiconductor index down about 8.5 percent on the jobs-report day, reminded investors that this is now a crowded and rate-sensitive trade.[4] Within our watchlist, Micron, Arm, Advanced Micro Devices, ALAB, SNDK, and IONQ all delivered double-digit weekly gains, while POET and TSEM lagged with notable declines, illustrating how investors are differentiating between secular beneficiaries, valuation extremes, and idiosyncratic execution risk.

Software and cloud infrastructure formed the second major axis of leadership. Our Software Infrastructure bucket saw outsized weekly gains from Snowflake, Elastic, Amplitude, GitLab, C3.ai, Palantir, Samsara, and Cloudflare, with Snowflake up about 48.4 percent over the week and 81.2 percent over the month, reflecting a decisive reset in sentiment following its AI platform repositioning and investor enthusiasm around consumption re-acceleration.[6] Elastic advanced about 18.0 percent on the week and 33.1 percent on the month, helped by its positioning as the “Search AI Company” and upcoming investor conferences that are expected to highlight its Search AI Platform for observability and security.[19] Datadog, another key observability and monitoring name, gained 11.3 percent on the week and 76.0 percent over the month, supported by its recent first-quarter earnings beat in which it reported earnings per share of 0.60 dollars, beating the consensus of 0.42 dollars by nearly 43 percent, confirming durable demand for cloud application monitoring and security capabilities.[16] These moves highlight the market’s increasing preference for data-plane and control-plane software that directly monetizes AI and cloud complexity.

Application software, especially workflow, productivity, and back-office platforms, delivered a significant catch-up move. Atlassian rose roughly 26.0 percent on the week and now carries a twelve-month price target of about 145.63 dollars, implying nearly 66 percent upside from its current price near 87.87 dollars, with a consensus rating of “Moderate Buy” from 28 analysts.[10] ServiceNow climbed 21.8 percent over the week and 36.4 percent over the month, supported by first-quarter subscription revenue of 3.671 billion dollars, representing 22 percent year-over-year growth and 19 percent growth in constant currency, reinforcing its status as a core AI-enabled workflow platform for large enterprises.[13] Oracle and IBM each gained roughly 17.5 percent and 17.3 percent respectively over the week, reflecting the market’s recognition that legacy enterprise vendors with scaled installed bases are now credible AI infrastructure and application platforms in their own right.[14][26] Oracle’s market capitalization stands near 579 billion dollars, with shares recently trading around 280.83 dollars, while IBM’s shares were recently quoted at approximately 253.23 dollars, with consensus twelve-month targets around 321 dollars and near-term institutional commentary centering on approximately 266.67 dollars per share.[14][26] These rallies underscore a broadening of AI monetization beyond pure-play hyperscalers and semis into full-stack enterprise platforms.

Within cybersecurity, performance was more polarized but directionally positive. Okta led the group with a roughly 33.6 percent weekly gain and 62.7 percent advance over the month, as investors looked ahead to its upcoming fourth-quarter and fiscal-year results release scheduled for early March 2026 and reevaluated the durability of its identity-platform moat.[7] CrowdStrike added about 10.2 percent on the week and 60.4 percent over the month, underpinned by its status as a leading endpoint protection and extended detection and response platform, and supported by a consensus “Buy” rating from 43 analysts and a price target near 673.65 dollars.[12] Palo Alto Networks rose about 8.1 percent for the week and 55.6 percent over the month, reflecting strong confidence in its platformization strategy and secure access service edge offerings. At the same time, Zscaler declined 23.4 percent on the week following a disappointing quarterly update that showed decelerating free cash flow margins and triggered a roughly 30 percent single-day share price decline, even as some fundamental investors argued that the stock’s post-selloff level near 127 dollars represented a long-term buying opportunity relative to their intrinsic value estimate around 185 dollars per share.[11] SentinelOne fell 11.5 percent on the week, highlighting the market’s increasingly discriminating stance toward security names where the path to scale profitability or product differentiation remains uncertain.

Adtech and digital media offered another dimension of leadership and dispersion. AppLovin surged about 27.3 percent over the week and 33.3 percent over the month, and currently trades near 483.44 dollars per share with a market backdrop that increasingly rewards its AI-enhanced advertising optimization and mobile gaming monetization capabilities.[9] Zeta Global gained 21.8 percent on the week and 23.1 percent on the month, signaling growing investor interest in AI-driven customer data platforms and marketing automation. By contrast, The Trade Desk fell about 3.7 percent over the week, and OMC, a more traditional agency and marketing conglomerate, declined roughly 3.0 percent, reflecting a subtle rotation favoring programmatic and performance-based advertising technologies over legacy media and agency exposures.

Cyclicals and real-economy sectors also participated in the week’s risk-on phases. United Airlines advanced about 14.8 percent on the week and 24.1 percent over the month; its shares recently traded around 103.24 dollars, with a market capitalization of 33.35 billion dollars and a price-to-earnings ratio near 9.78, suggesting that investors are increasingly comfortable underwriting a normalized air-travel demand environment and improved capital discipline in the airline industry.[22] Nucor, a bellwether steel and metals name, gained 7.8 percent on the week and 10.6 percent over the month, while Freeport-McMoRan rose about 6.0 percent and 16.2 percent over those periods, respectively, signaling constructive sentiment around industrial and copper demand. In energy, the picture was more mixed, with Devon Energy down 5.8 percent on the week and 12.0 percent over the month, while refiners like Valero and integrated producers such as Occidental saw more muted moves, reflecting the interplay between commodity prices, refining spreads, and expectations for demand growth.

Defensives and consumer staples underperformed as part of the rotation away from safety. Constellation Brands declined about 7.1 percent on the week and 9.2 percent over the month, while Clorox fell roughly 5.3 percent over the week even as it managed a modest 3.3 percent rise over the month, illustrating that staples are being used more as a funding source than as a return driver when risk appetite is high. The Clorox move was also influenced by stock-specific factors, but the broader pattern is consistent with rising real yields and a risk-on tilt that reduces the relative attractiveness of low-growth, bond-proxy equities.

## Top Movers & Earnings Recap

Among watchlist names, Snowflake delivered one of the most dramatic moves of the week. The stock gained approximately 48.4 percent over the week and 81.2 percent over the month, making it the standout in our Software Infrastructure bucket. ## Macro & Rates Environment

The macro backdrop this week was dominated by two interrelated themes: the durability of inflation and the trajectory of global and US monetary policy. J.P. Morgan’s global research team has highlighted that global inflation, which was earlier expected to remain relatively stable through 2026, is now facing renewed upward pressure from an energy price spike and strong global growth momentum.[25] This has stoked inflation, particularly in regions sensitive to commodity prices, and is paving the way for monetary policy tightening rather than easing in several developed markets.[25] The European Central Bank and the Bank of Japan, for example, are now expected to raise policy rates in June, following earlier action by the Reserve Bank of Australia, with further moves anticipated in Scandinavia and New Zealand in subsequent quarters.[25] While most of these dynamics are ex-US, they contribute to a global backdrop of higher-for-longer rates and upward pressure on long-term yields, which in turn affects US equity valuations and cross-border capital flows.

In the US, the federal funds rate remains in a restrictive range, and forward-looking expectations derived from Trading Economics models suggest that the policy rate is likely to be around 3.75 percent by the end of this quarter.[2] This implies a modest easing from the current effective rate but not a return to the near-zero environment that characterized much of the previous decade. Importantly, the recent strong jobs report, which catalyzed a sharp selloff in technology shares mid-week, reinforced the narrative that the labor market remains resilient and that the Fed has room to maintain a restrictive stance for longer.[4] The reaction in Treasury markets was swift: the 10-year yield climbed to about 4.54 percent, the 2-year to roughly 4.16 percent, and the 30-year to around 5.00 percent, levels that exert mechanical pressure on equity valuations, especially for longer-duration growth assets.[4]

The economic calendar itself has been relatively sparse in terms of transformative data surprises over the past week, with Trading Economics’ calendar showing the usual cadence of releases but no single print, apart from the labor data, fundamentally altering the growth narrative.[3] However, the tone of central bank communication has become more hawkish globally, and this is likely to increase the sensitivity of risk assets to incremental data on inflation, wages, and activity.[25] In particular, any signs that service inflation is re-accelerating or that wage growth is not moderating as expected could push terminal rate expectations higher, raising the discount rate applied to equity cash flows and potentially forcing a further de-rating of the highest-multiple segments of the market.

Against this backdrop, growth-sensitive and rate-sensitive sectors have become key barometers of macro sentiment. The sharp reversal in the Nasdaq 100 and the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index following the jobs report underscores how quickly sentiment can swing when yields move.[4][20] Conversely, the resilience of financials, select industrials, and airlines such as United Airlines suggests that the market is simultaneously comfortable with a soft-landing scenario in which growth remains solid even as inflation edges down only gradually.[22][25] This is consistent with the “no landing” or “soft but extended landing” narratives that have gained traction in recent months, where economic activity remains robust enough to support earnings, but not so strong as to force aggressive new rounds of tightening.

Looking forward, the interplay between inflation expectations, energy prices, and central bank policy will remain central. JP Morgan’s research notes that while rates across the globe have largely been on hold since the onset of recent geopolitical tensions, central bank rhetoric has shifted in a more hawkish direction, suggesting that further rate hikes may be on the horizon in multiple jurisdictions.[25] For US equities, this implies that the path of least resistance is not a rapid return to the ultra-accommodative policies of the late 2010s, but rather a prolonged period of real yields that are positive and non-trivial. In such a regime, equity returns are likely to be increasingly driven by earnings growth and cash-generation capability rather than multiple expansion alone, favoring companies with clear operating leverage to AI and digital transformation, tangible pricing power, and disciplined capital allocation.

## What To Watch Next Week

As we look ahead to next week, the primary question for US equities is whether this week’s volatility marks the beginning of a broader consolidation phase or simply a pause in an AI-led bull leg. The S&P 500’s recent record close and nine-day winning streak underscore the strength of the underlying uptrend, while the subsequent tech-led selloff triggered by a strong jobs report and higher yields highlights how quickly sentiment can swing when positioning is crowded and valuations are elevated.[1][4] The balance of evidence suggests that AI and digital transformation remain powerful structural drivers of earnings and multiple expansion, but that the path forward will be bumpier and more selective.

From a macro perspective, we will be watching incoming inflation and activity data for confirmation or rejection of the “higher-for-longer” rate narrative. If inflation data come in hotter than expected, or if wage growth shows signs of re-acceleration, markets may further price out rate cuts and push long-term yields higher, which would likely pressure high-multiple, long-duration growth names and favor financials, cyclicals, and value exposures.[2][3][25] Conversely, if inflation continues to trend lower and activity indicators suggest a gentle cooling of the labor market, markets may regain confidence that central banks can eventually ease without reigniting inflation, a scenario that would likely support a renewed rotation into quality growth and AI leaders. In either case, rate sensitivity will remain a key driver of factor and sector performance.

Within our watchlist, we will focus on the sustainability of this week’s outsized movers. For Snowflake, the key will be evidence of improving consumption trends and clear AI monetization pathways that justify the recent 48.4 percent weekly and 81.2 percent monthly gains.[6] For Okta, all eyes are on its upcoming earnings release and whether it can demonstrate re-accelerating growth and margin expansion sufficient to support the 62.7 percent monthly move.[7] Micron’s next updates, including its approaching Q3 fiscal 2026 earnings expected around late June, will be critical in validating the bullish memory-cycle thesis and the elevated price targets that now range into the 600–800 dollar zone.[8][5] In cybersecurity, the market will look for signs that Zscaler can stabilize after its sharp drawdown, while CrowdStrike and Palo Alto Networks will be monitored as potential relative winners in a consolidating field.[11][12]

We will also be closely watching the behavior of “second-derivative” AI beneficiaries such as Elastic, Datadog, Cloudflare, and Palantir. Each of these names offers leveraged exposure to AI adoption through data, observability, networking, or decision-intelligence layers, but they also trade at premium valuations that are vulnerable to shifts in sentiment.[16][19][29][15] In addition, quantum and high-performance compute plays like IonQ and select semiconductor names remain high-beta expressions of the AI theme that could either amplify gains or exacerbate drawdowns depending on the macro backdrop and investor risk appetite.[23][20] In more traditional sectors, United Airlines, Nucor, and Freeport-McMoRan will serve as barometers of cyclical momentum and investor confidence in the soft-landing narrative.[22]

For portfolio positioning, this environment argues for a barbell strategy that combines high-conviction AI and digital transformation beneficiaries with more traditional cyclicals and quality value names that benefit from resilient growth and higher yields. Within AI, we continue to favor companies with clear near-term earnings leverage and strong competitive moats, such as ServiceNow, Datadog, and CrowdStrike, alongside selectively adding to high-quality data and infrastructure platforms like Snowflake, Elastic, and Oracle on volatility.[13][16][12][6][19][14] At the same time, maintaining exposure to financials, industrials, and select materials can help cushion portfolios against rate-driven factor rotations and provide participation in any continued cyclical recovery. Risk management, including careful sizing of more speculative names like C3.ai, IonQ, and certain high-beta semiconductors, remains paramount.[28][23][20]

In sum, the week demonstrated that while AI continues to fuel Wall Street’s momentum, the market is entering a more mature phase of the cycle in which macro, rates, and valuation discipline matter as much as narrative. For buy-side investors, the opportunity set remains rich, but the easy, index-level gains from simply owning broad tech exposure are likely behind us for now. Generating alpha from here will require granular security selection, active risk management, and a willingness to lean into volatility when dislocations in high-quality names arise.
